summary: Initial intake to map Archipelago's private deployment constraints. Main topics: VPC topology (TGW vs peering), private endpoints, egress & country/region gating, KMS/HSM integration, audit requirements. Customer leaning toward Private deployment behind their VPC with strict egress rules and data residency needs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-03 15:00 UTC
Duration: 59 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (Redwood CSM); Tomás Ruiz (CTO Archipelago), Priya Desai (Lead Infra), Evan Moore (Security) - and Jae Kim (PM)

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Lena, AE at Redwood, Marcus our solutions engineer is here, and Sofia who'll help with onboarding. Can we go around quickly from you folks?
[00:12] Tomás Ruiz: Yeah, I'm Tomás, CTO. We run a data analytics platform, building some LLM products on top of our data lake. Trying to figure out how to bring inference into our private cloud for compliance and latency reasons.
[00:25] Priya Desai: Priya, infra lead. We'll be doing most of the networking work, peering, routing, egress controls, that sort of thing.
[00:31] Evan Moore: Evan, security architect. My priority is auditability, key management, and making sure no customer PII leaves allowed regions.
[00:38] Jae Kim: Hey, Jae, product. Mostly listening for constraints and timelines.

[02:10] Marcus Chen: Great, thanks. High level — we support three deployment models: hosted, dedicated reserved pools, and private where we deploy a private control plane and inference nodes that connect to your VPC via private endpoints. For this session let's map your network and requirements so we can propose the right private topology.

[03:05] Tomás: Right. We want a private deployment. The big constraints: we need everything in our AWS accounts (multiple accounts across us-east-1 and eu-west-1), traffic must not traverse the public internet, and we need to ensure logs are retained for 7 years for certain regulated customers. Also latency budget is about 200ms p50 for small completion requests.

[03:50] Marcus: Understood. A couple clarifying q's: do you currently use AWS Transit Gateway or is your team handling pairwise VPC peering? And any existing on-prem datacenter connectivity?
[04:05] Priya: We use TGW centrally for cross-account VPCs inside a region. We do have an on-prem site via Direct Connect that peers into the TGW. For eu-west-1 we have a separate TGW.

[04:30] Marcus: Good, TGW is usually cleaner for many VPCs. For cross-region we can run private endpoints in each region and control routing via TGW attachments. Important: private endpoints from Redwood will be AWS PrivateLink style — interface endpoints in your VPCs.

[05:10] Evan: Quick question — does Redwood need any inbound ports opened from the internet for control plane? We have to avoid any exposure.

[05:20] Lena: Short answer: with Private we can run a customer-managed VPC peering model where the control plane is reachable via PrivateLink, not the public internet. There is a small control-channel to Redwood's management plane if you choose our managed control plane; alternatively we can deploy a customer-owned control plane for air-gapped setups. Marcus do you want to expand?

[05:38] Marcus: Yeah, so two patterns: 1) Redwood-managed control plane with PrivateLink endpoints in your account — this keeps management traffic private; 2) Full customer-owned control plane (VMs/k8s) where Redwood provides an image and we do an on-prem install — that's for the most restrictive customers. For most enterprises TGW + PrivateLink is enough.

[06:50] Priya: If we use PrivateLink, who creates the endpoint service and who accepts? We need to know the exact ARNs because our security team automates acceptance.

[07:00] Marcus: Redwood will publish an endpoint service. We'll provide the service name and principals, and your team will create interface endpoints and accept the service in account. We can also support endpoint policies to restrict which subnets/roles can use it.

[07:30] Tomás: Sounds fine. About egress — we have strict egress filtering, only certain SNAT IPs allowed. Can Redwood work through NATed egress or do we need a static set of IP addresses for outbound calls?

[07:48] Marcus: For model fetching and telemetry, outbound from the inference nodes goes to Redwood storage and metrics endpoints. We can support routing via your NATs; if you require allow-listing we can provide a set of egress IPs per region for Dedicated/Hosted but for Private deployments where nodes sit inside your VPC the egress path is under your control and we don't require open internet if using PrivateLink to a Redwood endpoint. There's nuance: if you pick pull-based updates for model artifacts, you might need outbound to S3 or a signed URL. We can also push artifacts into an S3 bucket in your account via cross-account replication.

[09:05] Evan: KMS — we must manage keys for any persisted cache or logs with our KMS. Can Redwood integrate with customer-managed KMS or HSM?

[09:20] Marcus: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS for encryption-at-rest for model caches and logs. For HSM level there's a roadmap; we currently integrate with AWS KMS CMKs and can accept grants for access. We'll note HSM as a requirement and map it to our roadmap items.

[10:05] Priya: Data residency — some EU customers' data cannot leave eu-west-1. Can we pin models and runtime to region? Also, do you support region-specific hosting for embeddings?

[10:22] Lena: Absolutely. We can run inference nodes in eu-west-1 and keep KV caches and logs there. We have region-aware routing and can pin requests to regional clusters. For model variants, we can replicate weights to that region or use quantized variants to save space. Marcus will follow-up with exact storage footprint.

[11:00] Marcus: To add — if you need strict residency, we recommend Dedicated in-region pools or Private nodes in your accounts to avoid cross-region fallbacks. We also offer automatic fallback policies but they can be disabled per customer.

[12:05] Jae: On timelines — if we greenlight, how long to spin up a Private deployment in two regions?

[12:20] Marcus: Typical timeline: with our managed private control plane and your team's help for endpoint creation, ~4–6 weeks to MVP (basic endpoints, networking, IAM, and test dataset). If you want customer-owned control plane and strict approvals, add another 4–6 weeks.

[13:10] Tomás: Cost question — what drives costs for private? GPUs obviously, but also networking and egress if cross-region. Any ballpark?

[13:30] Lena: Costs are a combo: reserved node capacity or per-node usage, model size impacts memory/GPU type, and storage/traffic. We'll put together a back-of-envelope for your expected RPS and token mix. Marcus can do the performance estimate after we get your usage profile.

[14:25] Priya: We have a couple of technical points: 1) our VPC CIDRs overlap with some partner networks, we use NAT for outbound. 2) We run kube clusters in private subnets with strict SGs. Will Redwood require specific SG ports?

[14:45] Marcus: For interface endpoints — it's TCP 443 to the PrivateLink interface. For intra-VPC traffic between your app and the inference nodes, it's also HTTPS. We may require some agent for metrics that uses outbound TCP 443. No open inbound 22 or other management ports.

[15:40] Evan: Audit logs: we need proof that inference requests containing PII are scrubbed at rest or logged with redaction. What logs does Redwood produce and can we push them to our CloudWatch/ELK?

[16:00] Marcus: We produce request-level telemetry (traces, latencies), and can provide configurable request logging. For sensitive data, we recommend a redaction layer in your app or use tokenization before sending. We can forward logs to your S3/CloudWatch via cross-account role so logs never sit in Redwood-managed buckets unless you opt in.

[17:10] Tomás: How do you handle secret management for API keys when we use the private model endpoints? Do we store keys locally?

[17:26] Lena: For Private deployments, authentication can be integrated via mTLS or short-lived tokens issued by your IDP. We also support API keys stored in your KMS via grants — nothing has to live in plaintext in Redwood's control plane.

[18:05] Priya: Can we do mutual TLS for node-to-node? Our security team prefers mTLS for all inter-service communication.

[18:18] Marcus: Yes, mTLS is supported between components. For Redwood-managed nodes we terminate at the PrivateLink interface; we can establish mTLS over those connections. For customer-managed control plane we can provide certs for mutual TLS.

[19:30] Jae: One more on routing: if a request originates in eu-west-1 but the preferred model only exists in us-east-1, will Redwood route across regions? We can't allow that for certain customers.

[19:45] Marcus: By default we try to route to local regional clusters. If model variant isn't present we can either 1) fail with a clear error, 2) redirect to a fallback in another region (if you allow), or 3) pre-stage the model in that region. You'd configure a policy per environment.

[20:20] Evan: For the audit trail, do you provide cryptographic checksums of model binaries and the exact runtime used for a given request so we can reproduce results if needed?

[20:35] Marcus: Yes, we store model version IDs, quantization profile, runtime kernel build info, and those are included in trace metadata for each request. We can surface artifact checksums on demand.

[21:40] Priya: We have a specific networking ask: subnets in eu-west-1 are private with no IGW. Our egress is via TGW to a centralized NAT account that SNATs to a pool of Elastic IPs. Will that work?

[21:55] Marcus: That's a common pattern. Your inference nodes can live in private subnets, utilize the NAT pool for any necessary outbound, and the interface endpoint via PrivateLink for Redwood management. If you need allow-listing, we can provide specifics for any required outbound hostnames or IPs, though we prefer PrivateLink so outbound isn't necessary.

[23:10] Tomás: Regarding capacity — how do we do autoscaling while ensuring compliance? We don't want nodes to burst into another region or onto GPUs we haven't vetted.

[23:28] Marcus: Autoscaling policies are configurable by you. For Private we can constrain scaling to specific instance families/AZs/regions. For Dedicated we reserve capacity so scaling stays within committed nodes. We can also surface alerts when scaling would breach policy.

[24:50] Evan: A compliance nuance: some customers require FIPS-compliant TLS and specific cipher suites. Can Redwood support that?

[25:03] Marcus: We support FIPS endpoints and can configure cipher suites. For customer-managed control plane you have full control over TLS config. For our managed plane we offer FIPS-compliant endpoints in certain regions — we'll confirm which ones in the security pack.

[26:15] Priya: Anything we should prepare on our side to make onboarding faster?

[26:25] Lena: Yes — 1) List of VPC CIDRs and which accounts/regions; 2) TGW attachments and Direct Connect info; 3) KMS key ARNs and HSM needs; 4) compliance docs you want (SOC2/ISO) — we'll map those. If you share those we can produce a bespoke network runbook.

[27:40] Priya: We'll compile that. Also, do you have any prebuilt IaC modules (CloudFormation/Terraform) for the interface endpoints acceptance?

[27:50] Marcus: We have Terraform modules and CloudFormation snippets for endpoint creation and IAM roles. We'll share a repo link.

[29:05] Jae: On governance, who has access to change endpoint acceptance? We want a strictly audited process.

[29:15] Lena: That stays with your security/infra: acceptance of endpoint service is an account-level action. We recommend using an automated approval workflow that requires a PR and tag from your security team — we can provide templates.

[31:00] Tomás: Performance — if we run a 256-token context and expect 100 requests per second, what GPU class do you recommend?

[31:12] Marcus: Quick callback: models and batch patterns change recommendations. But rough rule: for a 7B model at 256 context, a single A10G-equivalent could handle somewhere between 100–200 RPS depending on batching and KV cache hit rate. We'll do a proper perf estimate with your expected token mix.

[32:05] Evan: Do you support prefix caching or per-customer KV caches to reduce cost?

[32:15] Marcus: Yes, KV caches and prefix caching are part of the runtime. For Private we can host caches in your account so cache data never leaves region.

[33:40] Priya: If we run caches in our account, any special storage requirements? Like EBS vs instance storage?

[33:50] Marcus: Caches can be on instance-local NVMe for perf, or EBS for persistence. We'll recommend NVMe for hot caches; we'll document disk sizing per model.

[35:05] Tomás: On SSO and RBAC for the console — we need SAML/Okta integration and granular roles for who can deploy models or change rollout policies.

[35:20] Lena: We support SAML SSO (Okta), SCIM provisioning, and role-based access controls with audit logs. For Private deployments with Redwood-managed console we can integrate your IdP; for customer-owned consoles you fully control RBAC.

[36:40] Priya: We want to test a P0 path: simple request flow from our private app to Redwood endpoint with strict logging enabled and no cross-region routing. Can you outline a minimal test?

[36:55] Marcus: Minimal test steps: 1) Create interface endpoint in a test VPC subnet and accept service; 2) Spin up a small test instance in same VPC/subnet; 3) Configure security group to only allow HTTPS to the endpoint; 4) Send a small test request to a non-production model pinned to the region; 5) Validate logs forwarded to your CloudWatch and trace metadata present. We'll provide the exact curl and IAM role snippets.

[38:10] Jae: Timeline-wise, if we get the artifacts to you this week, can we have the test environment in two weeks?

[38:20] Marcus: Yes, two weeks is feasible for a small test if we get the network artifacts and permission to create the interface endpoints. We'll schedule a hands-on workshop for the endpoint acceptance step.

[39:30] Lena: A few more compliance bits — Evan, you mentioned 7-year retention. That can be supported but may require dedicated storage in your account. We'll note retention policies and costs.

[40:05] Evan: Also encryption in transit & at rest must use our CMKs where possible.

[40:12] Marcus: Noted. We'll map which artifacts can be encrypted with your CMKs — caches, logs, and snapshots.

[41:20] Priya: One weird networking situation — one of our partner networks uses overlapping RFC1918 space and we sometimes route via NAT to an ISP. Could that break PrivateLink connections?

[41:35] Marcus: PrivateLink uses ENIs in your subnets; as long as the route to the endpoint's ENI is reachable and SGs allow it, it should work. Overlapping CIDRs are more of a peering/TGW problem; sometimes we recommend a proxy VPC or NAT translation. We can propose a design pattern to avoid overlaps.

[43:00] Tomás: Any legal or procurement items upfront? We may need a data processing addendum (DPA) and certain security attachments.

[43:12] Lena: We have a standard DPA and enterprise addendum. I'll send the DPA and SOC2 summary as part of the security pack. For more bespoke terms we can route to legal; procurement timeline typically adds 2–4 weeks.

[44:30] Priya: For the follow-up deep dive, can we focus on TGW routing specifics, route table examples, and Terraform snippets for endpoint creation?

[44:45] Marcus: Absolutely. We'll prepare route table diagrams showing TGW attachments, endpoint subnets, and example route entries. Also provide Terraform module links.

[46:05] Jae: Any immediate blockers?

[46:12] Priya: We need the exact AWS account IDs and endpoint service names to automate acceptance. Also we need confirmation on whether Redwood requires any IAM role in our account beyond an assume-role for log export.

[46:30] Lena: We'll provide those. For logs we usually ask for a cross-account role with limited permissions to write to a customer bucket; we can also push a signed package you can pull so no role is required. We'll include both options.

[47:55] Tomás: Let's talk SLAs briefly — for private deployments what uptime do you guarantee?

[48:10] Lena: For Private deployments with Dedicated reserved pools we offer SLA-backed uptime for inference endpoints. For customer-owned control plane SLAs depend on the customer's infra. We'll include SLA language in the proposal.

[49:05] Evan: On incident response — if there's a security incident, what's the escalation path and data access timeline?

[49:20] Sofia Alvarez: We have an incident response runbook for enterprise customers: 1) Triage within 1 hour, 2) initial report within 4 hours, 3) follow-ups and evidence within 48 hours depending on severity. We'll include contacts in the security pack.

[50:40] Marcus: Quick note on kernel/runtime: our inference runtime supports continuous batching and KV cache management which improves throughput; that means your effective RPS can be higher with higher cache hit rates. We'll quantify during the perf estimate.

[51:30] Priya: Ok, next steps recap?

[51:40] Lena: Recap — 1) We'll send the security pack (SOC2 summary, DPA, architecture notes), 2) Marcus will produce a performance/cost estimate based on 100 RPS 256-token workload, 3) Provide Terraform snippets and endpoint service ARNs, 4) Schedule hands-on workshop for interface endpoint acceptance and TGW route table walkthrough.

[52:10] Tomás: Sounds good. We'll gather VPC CIDRs, TGW attachments, KMS ARNs and send to Lena by 2027-05-06.

[52:26] Evan: One last clarifying thing — for logs retention, if we push logs to our S3 via cross-account, does Redwood keep any copies?

[52:40] Marcus: No, if logs are configured to be pushed to your account, Redwood doesn't retain additional copies unless you opt into using Redwood-managed storage. We'll ensure the default is zero-copy into your buckets.

[53:15] Jae: Great, thanks everyone.

[53:20] Lena: Thanks — we'll follow up with all artifacts.

[53:35] Tomás: Appreciate it.

[54:00] Meeting end.

Notes: transcript contains a few speech recognition glitches (proper noun spellings, occasional word swaps). Some technical terms abbreviated casually (TGW, KMS, CMK, NVMe).
